read.sections.0.text.note: God is พระผู้เป็นเจ้า with the verb ทรงสร้าง (KEY_TERMS asks to check that both read right to Muslim and Christian readers). "ancestral beings who shaped the land" is บรรพชนในตำนานที่สร้างรูปร่างของแผ่นดิน แหล่งน้ำ และสัตว์ต่างๆ; check "shaped". "the heavens and the earth" is ฟ้าและแผ่นดิน.
read.sections.0.text.source: People all over the world have asked where the world came from. Many communities have an origin account. It tells how something began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe that God created the heavens and the earth. Many Hindus see time as a great cycle. In this cycle, the universe is made, ends and then begins again. Many Aboriginal peoples of Australia tell of ancestral beings who shaped the land, the water and the animals. Groups in Africa, the Americas and the Pacific also pass on their own accounts in stories and songs. Even a small town can have an origin account, like the founding story of Tallgrass Valley. Accounts like these carry a group's beliefs and values.
read.sections.0.text.back: People all over the world have wondered where the world came from. Many communities have origin accounts, which tell how something began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe that God created the heavens and the earth. Many Hindus see time as a great cycle; in this cycle the universe is created, ends, and then begins again. Many Aboriginal Australians tell of ancestral beings who shaped the land, the waterholes and the animals. Groups in Africa, the Americas and the Pacific islands also pass on their own accounts through stories and songs. Even a small town can have an origin account, such as the founding story of Tallgrass Valley. Accounts like these hold a group's beliefs and values.

read.sections.0.simpler.note: Simpler says พระผู้เป็นเจ้าทรงสร้างโลก and บรรพชนในตำนาน; check with faith reviewers too.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: People all over the world ask how it all began. Many groups have an origin account. It tells how things began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe God made the world. Many Hindus believe the world ends and starts again. This happens again and again. In Australia, many Aboriginal people tell of beings from long ago. These beings made the land and the animals. Groups in Africa and the Pacific have their own accounts. Our made-up town, Tallgrass Valley, has one too. These accounts hold beliefs and values.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: People all over the world wonder how everything began. Many groups have origin accounts, which tell how things began. Many Muslims, Christians and Jews believe God created the world. Many Hindus believe the world ends and then begins again. This happens again and again. In Australia, many Aboriginal people tell of ancestral beings. These ancestral beings made the land and the animals. People in Africa and the Pacific also have their own accounts. Our fictional town, Tallgrass Valley, has one too. These accounts hold beliefs and values.

read.sections.1.text.note: "faith accounts" is คำอธิบายทางความเชื่อ, "cultural accounts" คำอธิบายทางวัฒนธรรม, "science account" คำอธิบายทางวิทยาศาสตร์. ทางศาสนา is an alternative for "faith", but would not fit Aboriginal accounts as well. Check.
read.sections.1.text.source: Each kind of account can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in nature. They use evidence that people can see, measure and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and has been growing ever since. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer other questions. Why is there a world? What matters most? How should people treat each other? Historians ask a third kind of question: who told an account, when, and why. Look again at the three questions about beginnings. Each one needs a different kind of answer.
read.sections.1.text.back: Each kind of account can answer questions in its own way. Scientists ask how things in nature came to be. They use evidence that people can see, measure and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since. Faith accounts and cultural accounts often answer other questions: Why is there a world? What matters most? How should people treat each other? Historians ask a third kind of question: who told the account, when, and why. Look at the three questions about beginnings again. Each one needs a different kind of answer.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Each account can answer its own kind of question. Scientists ask how things happen in nature. They use evidence they can see and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. Faith accounts often ask other things. Why is there a world? How should we live? Historians ask who told an account, and why. Each question needs its own kind of answer.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Each kind of account can answer its own questions. Scientists ask how things in nature came to be. They use evidence they can see and test. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. Faith accounts often ask about other things. Why is there a world? How should we live? Historians ask who told the account, and why. Each question needs a different kind of answer.

read.sections.2.heading.source: We learn about accounts with respect

read.sections.2.text.note: "people of faith" is ผู้มีศรัทธาในศาสนา; "Many people believe ..." is หลายคนเชื่อว่า...; check both are respectful and neutral. Review: "Many people hold both a faith account and a science account" is หลายคนยึดถือทั้ง...; ยึดถือ is fairly strong ("hold fast to"). Check it reads naturally beside ยอมรับ (accept) in the simpler text.
read.sections.2.text.source: In this lesson, we learn about accounts, but we do not judge them or rank them. Respect means describing each account carefully and never mocking it. We say "Many people believe ..." for a faith account and "Scientists explain ..." for a science account. Many people hold both a faith account and a science account, and many scientists are also people of faith. Nobody has to share what they believe. If you are not sure how to describe an account, check a trusted source or ask a teacher.
read.sections.2.text.back: In this lesson we learn about different accounts, but we don't judge or rank them. Respect means explaining each one carefully and never mocking it. We say "Many people believe..." for faith accounts and "Scientists explain..." for scientific accounts. Many people hold both faith accounts and scientific accounts, and many scientists are also people of religious faith. Nobody has to say what they believe. If you are not sure how to explain something, check a reliable source or ask your teacher.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Here, we learn about accounts. We do not judge them. We do not say one is best. Respect means we describe each account with care. We never laugh at it. Say "Many people believe" for faith. Say "Scientists explain" for science. Many people accept both kinds of account. You do not have to share your own beliefs.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: In this lesson, we learn about different accounts. We don't judge them. We don't say which one is best. Respect is explaining with care. We never laugh at them. Say "Many people believe" when talking about beliefs. Say "Scientists explain" when talking about science. Many people accept both kinds of account. You don't have to say your own beliefs.

write.example.source: The first question asks how the stars and the Earth formed. To answer it, people could use evidence that scientists measure. For example, they study light from faraway stars. The second question asks what the Tallgrass story teaches about sharing. To answer it, people could listen to the elders. They could think about the promise to share the fig tree. These questions need different answers. One asks how something happened in nature. The other asks what matters to a group of people.
write.example.back: The first question asks how the stars and the Earth came to be. To answer this question, people might use evidence scientists can measure. For example, scientists study light from very distant stars. The second question asks what the Tallgrass story teaches about sharing. To answer this question, people might listen to the elders tell it, and might think about the promise to share the fig tree's fruit. These questions need different answers. One asks how something happened in nature. The other asks what matters to a group of people.

watch.summary.source: This video gives a science account of how the universe began. Scientists explain that it began about 13.8 billion years ago. At first, it was very small and very hot. Since then, it has grown bigger and cooler. Scientists use evidence they can measure. For example, they see that faraway groups of stars are moving away from us. This shows that the universe is still growing. They also find a faint glow left over from when the universe was very young. A science account like this answers questions about how things happen in nature. Questions about meaning, or about how to live, need other kinds of answers. Many people value both a science account and a faith account.
watch.summary.back: This video gives a scientific explanation of how the universe began. Scientists explain that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. At first it was very small and very hot. Since then it has grown bigger and cooled down. Scientists use evidence that can be measured. For example, they see that very distant groups of stars are moving away from us. This shows the universe is still expanding. They have also found faint light left over from when the universe was very young. A scientific account like this answers the question of how things in nature came to be. Questions about meaning, or about how to live, need a different kind of answer. Many people value both scientific accounts and faith accounts.
